newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana mops up after Danny's unwanted visit.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana mops up after Danny's unwanted visit.

text.p: South Louisiana's tourism industry prides itself on its spicy hospitality that draws thousands, but Hurricane Danny was an unwanted visitor Friday.
"We had tourists all over the place, with room for a few more, but Danny we didn't want," said marina owner Butch Gaspard of Grand Isle, La. "He was a party-crasher."

Gaspard and hundreds of other southeast Louisiana coastal residents began mopping up Saturday as Danny moved east along the Gulf Coast, it reminding them that even minimal hurricanes can deliver a stinging slap.

Although the storm only teased New Orleans, the state's major tourist destination, with gusty breezes and scattered showers, Grand Isle was innundated with water driven onto the island from the north after the winds shifted.
To the west, in Plaquemines parish, more than two dozen trailer homes were heavily damaged, along with more than 100 boats and at least 17 helicopters.

Many of the 200 Grand Isle residents who ignored Thursday's evacuation order regretted that decision. "Next time somebody says even a baby hurricane is in the Gulf, you can bet they won't be buying beer, playing cards or sitting on their thumbs. You can bet they gonna be out of here," Mayor Pro Tem Ray Santini said.
Officials said wind and wave action from the storm exacerbated existing erosion problems on the fragile barrier island. "It's hard to tell yet just how much more land we lost," Santini said.

In lower Plaquemines, the "toe" on the boot-shaped Louisiana coastline, officials believe a tornado trashed 100 boats in the Buras, La., marina, many of them uninsured commercial shrimpers, Parish Council President Clyde Giordano said. A 10,000-gallon diesel tank overturned, worsening problems caused by fuel leaking from capsized vessels.

Quickly rising water at the Petroleum Helicopters Inc. facility in Venice, La., trapped at least 17 helicopters before they could be moved to higher ground. The business services off-shore drilling platforms.

Heavy rains and wind-driven water led officials in Plaquemines and St. Bernard parishes to close the only roads to areas outside hurricane protection levees, forcing those who did not flee soon enough to ride out the storm at home.

"We've got some problems, but -- thank God -- not that many," said St. Bernard Emergency Preparedness Director Bob Broccamonte. "I had 25 feet of water in my home in (Hurricane) Betsy in 1965. This is nothing."
